summary: In Greek mythology Pallas was one of the Gigantes, earthborn offspring of Gaia from the blood of castrated Uranus. Apollodorus says that in the Gigantomachy Athena flayed him and used his skin as a shield. A fragment of Epicharmus has Athena take her epithet "Pallas" from this kill. The atlas node is distinct from the Titan `pallas` (son of Crius) and from the Athenian `pallas-pandionid`.
etymology: Ancient Greek Pállas (Πάλλας). One aetiology of Athena's title "Pallas" derives it from this Giant after she flayed him for her cloak or aegis.

sections.heading: Gigantomachy
paragraphs: Apollodorus names Pallas among the Giants destroyed when the Olympians, aided by Heracles, fought the earthborn. Athena flays him and wears his skin as a shield in the fight. Epicharmus already linked Athena's name "Pallas" to that flaying.

The motif belongs to a family of stories in which Athena kills and skins an opponent for the aegis: Euripides has her flay "the Gorgon" at Phlegra; the epic Meropis has her flay the Giant Asterus. Another adversary also named Pallas — said to be Athena's father who tried to rape her — is a separate aetiology and is not this Gigantomachy figure.

sections.heading: Later art and homonyms
paragraphs: Claudian's late Latin Gigantomachia has Minerva's Gorgon shield turn Giants to stone; Pallas cries out as he petrifies. Keep this creature node apart from Titan `pallas` (Styx's consort, father of Nike and her siblings) and from `pallas-pandionid` of the Attic royal house.
